short: The first rhomboid tank, whose trials won the order that became the Mark I.
full:
After Little Willie failed to meet the War Office requirement to cross an eight-foot trench and climb a four-and-a-half-foot parapet, William Tritton and Walter Gordon Wilson designed a second machine with its tracks carried all the way around a rhomboid hull. It was built at Foster's of Lincoln under the cover description of a water carrier for Mesopotamia, and was known as Big Willie and then Mother, officially His Majesty's Land Ship Centipede. It first moved under its own power in January 1916, carrying a 6-pounder naval gun in a sponson on each side.

Trials at Hatfield Park opened with a private demonstration on 29 January 1916 and an official one on 2 February before Kitchener, Lloyd George and Balfour; George V watched on 8 February. An order for 100 machines followed on 12 February and was raised to 150 in April. Those production machines were the Mark I, which fought at Flers-Courcelette that September. Mother herself never went to war. She was kept for trials and training at Bovington and disappeared during the scrap drives of the Second World War.
